claims.text: The onset of premelting and melting in HEA nanoparticles is governed primarily by surface segregation of lower-melting-point constituent elements.
Nanoparticles with surfaces enriched in lower-melting components initiate melting at lower temperatures than nanoparticles with more homogeneous surfaces.
High-temperature annealing can minimize surface segregation and produce a more uniform surface composition.
Rapid quenching can preserve kinetic segregation that enriches the surface in lower-melting-point elements.
Differences in mixing enthalpy contribute to preferential migration of lower-melting components to the nanoparticle surface during rapid cooling.
Differences in atomic size contribute to preferential migration of lower-melting components to the nanoparticle surface during rapid cooling.
Surface enrichment in lower-melting components reduces local cohesive energy.
Reduced local cohesive energy lowers the energy barrier for atomic mobility.
A lower barrier for atomic mobility causes premelting to begin at a lower temperature.
Particles with homogeneous surface compositions require higher temperatures for melting to commence.
Quenched, surface-segregated samples will exhibit a lower premelting onset temperature than annealed, homogenized samples.
Quenched, surface-segregated samples will undergo the overall melting transition earlier than annealed, homogenized samples.
Surface-segregated samples will show a DSC melting peak shifted toward lower temperatures relative to homogenized samples.
The proposed relationship should hold for HEA nanoparticles approximately 5–50 nm in size.
The proposed relationship should hold for compositions having marked differences among the melting points of their constituent elements.
Marked differences in constituent melting points force surface segregation.
Outside the stated size and composition ranges, particle interactions or interface-energy variations may dominate melting behavior.
The magnitude of the temperature shift and degree of premelting are sensitive to nanoparticle size distribution and kinetic barriers.
